# Problem 1

```{r problem1}
# Function to check whether at least two people share a birthday
birthday_sim = function(n) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}

# Run 10,000 simulations for each group size
set.seed(123)

birthday_results = 
  tibble(group_size = 2:50) |>
  mutate(
    probability = map_dbl(
      group_size,
      ~ mean(replicate(10000, birthday_sim(.x)))
    )
  )

# Plot the estimated probabilities
birthday_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of Shared Birthdays by Group Size",
    x = "Group Size",
    y = "Probability of at Least One Shared Birthday"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The probability of at least two people sharing a birthday increases with group size. At around 23 people, the probability exceeds 50%, illustrating the birthday paradox. By 50 people, the probability is approximately 97%. The increase gradually slows as the probability approaches 1.

# Problem 2

```{r problem2}
# List all participant files
file_df = tibble(
  file_name = list.files(
    path = "data",
    pattern = "\\.csv$"
  )
)

# Read each participant's data using purrr::map
participant_data = file_df |>
  mutate(
    data = map(
      file_name,
      ~ read_csv(
        file.path("data", .x),
        show_col_types = FALSE
      )
    )
  )

# Extract subject ID and study arm, then tidy weekly observations
longitudinal_data = participant_data |>
  mutate(
    arm = case_when(
      str_starts(file_name, "con") ~ "Control",
      str_starts(file_name, "exp") ~ "Experimental"
    ),
    subject_id = str_remove(file_name, "\\.csv$") |>
      str_remove("^(con|exp)_")
  ) |>
  select(subject_id, arm, data) |>
  unnest(data) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "observation",
    names_prefix = "week_"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.numeric(week),
    arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Control", "Experimental"))
  )

# Spaghetti plot
longitudinal_data |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = week,
      y = observation,
      group = interaction(arm, subject_id),
      color = arm
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  facet_grid(. ~ arm) +
  labs(
    title = "Longitudinal Observations by Study Arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Study Arm"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The spaghetti plot shows distinct trends between the two study arms. Observations in the control group fluctuate over time without a clear upward or downward trend. In contrast, most participants in the experimental group show increasing observations over the eight weeks. Although there is individual variability within both groups, the experimental group demonstrates a more pronounced upward trend compared with the relatively stable control group.

# Problem 3 


```{r problem3, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
# Set simulation parameters
set.seed(123)

n = 30
sigma = 5
mu_values = 0:6
n_sim = 5000

# Function to simulate one dataset and perform a t-test
simulate_t_test = function(mu) {
  sample_data = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

  t.test(sample_data, mu = 0) |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(estimate, p.value)
}

# Run 5000 simulations for each true mean
simulation_results =
  tibble(mu = mu_values) |>
  mutate(
    results = map(
      mu,
      \(true_mu) map_dfr(
        1:n_sim,
        \(i) simulate_t_test(true_mu)
      )
    )
  ) |>
  unnest(results) |>
  mutate(rejected = p.value < 0.05)

# Calculate statistical power
power_results =
  simulation_results |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarize(
    power = mean(rejected),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot power against true mean
power_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = power)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Power by True Mean",
    x = "True Mean (mu)",
    y = "Power"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = mu_values) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_minimal()

# Calculate average estimates across all and rejected samples
estimate_results =
  simulation_results |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarize(
    all_samples = mean(estimate),
    rejected_samples = mean(estimate[rejected]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(all_samples, rejected_samples),
    names_to = "sample_type",
    values_to = "mean_estimate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    sample_type = recode(
      sample_type,
      all_samples = "All Samples",
      rejected_samples = "Rejected Samples Only"
    )
  )

# Compare average estimates with true means
estimate_results |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = mu,
    y = mean_estimate,
    color = sample_type
  )) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50"
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimated Mean vs. True Mean",
    x = "True Mean (mu)",
    y = "Average Estimated Mean",
    color = "Sample Type"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = mu_values) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Power and Effect Size**

The statistical power increases as the true mean moves farther away from the null value of zero. When the true mean is zero, the rejection rate is approximately 0.05, consistent with the significance level. As the effect size increases, the test becomes more likely to reject the null hypothesis, with power approaching 1 for larger values of the true mean.

**Average Estimated Mean**

The average estimated mean across all simulated samples is approximately equal to the true mean, indicating that the sample mean is an unbiased estimator. However, when considering only samples in which the null hypothesis is rejected, the average estimate tends to be larger than the true mean for smaller positive effect sizes. This occurs because statistically significant results are more likely to arise from samples with unusually large estimated effects. As power increases, this selection bias becomes smaller, and the average estimate among rejected samples approaches the true mean.
